title: Children's hospital asthma pathway: action plan completeness and 90-day emergency revisits, accepted with one gate met and one unmet
notes: Ordinary path on a clearly stated cohort question. The fixture search returns seven records with abstracts; the appraisal (shape appraisal) annotates all seven and records five source-derived claims whose passages are exact substrings of the abstracts, with certainty 'low' as the appraisal's own value. The design decision rests on claims c1, c2, c3 and c5; its ethics gate is met on the investigator's REB approval record and its data sharing gate is unmet (the custodian returned the draft unsigned), so acceptance succeeds (selectionStatus accepted) while the action stays blocked (actionStatus blocked), in the store, on screen and in the export (G7; A2 item 9). The problem reply omits the constraints key, so the investigator's constraints stay as typed (G11). Record ids are not typed by hand: each is stableRecordId(record) imported from src/lib/evidence/records.ts in the author's generator script: 'ev-' plus the base-36 FNV-1a hash of the normalised DOI (records 1, 3, 4, 6: ev-0lz2pd5, ev-1dlrmal, ev-0i10rm2, ev-04pzwqi) or, without a DOI, of titleYearKey(title, year) (records 2, 5, 7: ev-0nqmzqb, ev-0bs8ux6, ev-1w4t8sp). Requires S13 (appraisal payload applied on the production scan path), S11 (selectionStatus, actionStatus, basis on acceptance) and D5 (decision status text on screen). Catches: an unmet gate treated as met or ignored at acceptance, acceptance refused because a gate is unresolved, an action shown as ready while a gate is unmet, and export or reload that loses the gate statuses. The audit checks fail at 875fe59 because of the audit merge defect (A3 L1.6).

inputs.need:
I am a paediatric respirologist and the physician lead for the asthma pathway at a 190-bed children's hospital. We admit about 620 children aged 2 to 17 with asthma each year. Every child is supposed to go home with a written asthma action plan on our five-section paper template (daily medicines, signs of worsening, what to do in the yellow zone, when to come back to emergency, and a booked follow-up appointment), which is scanned into the chart. When our respiratory educator looked at 90 plans from last winter, 41 were missing at least one section, most often the yellow-zone steps or the follow-up appointment.

Our families come back a lot: roughly one in six children has another asthma visit to an emergency department within 90 days, and some of those visits are to the community hospitals nearer home, which we never hear about. Before we spend money on an electronic plan with forced fields, I want to know whether a complete plan at discharge is actually associated with fewer emergency revisits and readmissions within 90 days, or whether complete plans simply go to families who were going to do well anyway.

We would like to do a cohort study of discharges from 2022 to 2025, with plan completeness scored from the scanned template and revisits taken from the provincial emergency visits dataset so that visits to other hospitals are counted. I need help defining completeness, choosing the confounders that matter (severity of the admission, previous admissions, age, controller medicine at discharge, neighbourhood income), checking whether four years of discharges give enough events, and working out what we can say if the linkage is delayed. Our ethics approval is in place, but the data sharing agreement with the provincial custodian is not.
inputs.constraints: No new funding. The analysis is done by me and a data analyst at 0.2 FTE over six months. Data come only from the hospital chart archive and the provincial emergency visits dataset; there is no contact with families.

response.title: Written asthma action plan completeness at discharge and 90-day emergency revisits in children
response.subtitle: Cohort of 2022 to 2025 discharges linked to provincial emergency visits
response.statement: Children admitted with asthma are meant to leave with a complete five-section written action plan, but a local review found 41 of 90 plans missing at least one section. It is not known whether a complete plan at discharge is associated with fewer asthma emergency revisits or readmissions within 90 days once severity, previous admissions and family circumstances are taken into account. The answer decides whether an electronic plan with forced fields is worth funding.
response.whoAffected: Children aged 2 to 17 admitted with asthma (about 620 a year), their parents and caregivers, the respiratory educators and ward nurses who write the plans, and the community hospitals that see revisits the children's hospital never learns about.
response.whatHurts: An emergency revisit means another night of breathlessness, missed school and work, and sometimes a readmission. Incomplete plans leave families without clear steps for the yellow zone or a booked follow-up, and families with limited English may be least able to fill the gaps themselves.
response.currentPractice: A five-section paper plan is written at discharge by the ward nurse or respiratory educator and scanned into the chart. Completeness is not measured routinely, and revisits to other hospitals are invisible to the discharging team.
response.whyNow: A proposal for an electronic plan with forced fields is waiting for funding, the winter review showed frequent missing sections, and ethics approval for secondary use of charts has just been granted.
response.patientCenteredGoal: Every child goes home with a plan the family can use, and fewer children need emergency care for asthma in the three months after discharge.
response.summary: Problem framed as a cohort question: is a complete action plan at discharge associated with fewer 90-day asthma emergency revisits after accounting for severity and family circumstances?

steps.query: written asthma action plan completeness at paediatric discharge and emergency revisits within 90 days

records.title: Completeness of written asthma action plans at discharge and 90-day emergency revisits in children: a provincial cohort
records.authors: Achterberg-Mensah L, Delacroix-Oyelowo T, Brandvold-Ng S
records.abstract: We followed 2,340 children aged 2 to 17 discharged after an asthma admission from four hospitals and linked them to provincial emergency department data for 90 days. Plans were scored complete when all five template sections were filled, which happened at 52 percent of discharges. After adjustment for age, prior admissions, admission severity and controller prescription, a complete plan was associated with fewer emergency revisits within 90 days (adjusted hazard ratio 0.72, 95 percent CI 0.58 to 0.89). The association was weaker in children with a previous intensive care admission. Revisits to hospitals other than the discharging hospital made up a fifth of all events. Residual confounding by family engagement cannot be excluded, because families who keep appointments may also receive more complete plans.

records.title: Raising action plan completeness on a paediatric ward: a before-and-after improvement report
records.abstract: On one 28-bed paediatric ward, a nurse-led discharge checklist and weekly feedback raised the proportion of complete asthma action plans from 48 percent to 86 percent over nine months. Emergency revisits within 30 days were 11 percent before and 9 percent after the change, a difference the authors describe as compatible with chance given 210 and 196 discharges in the two periods. Completion fell to 71 percent in the three months after feedback stopped. Parents reported that the yellow-zone section was the part most often explained in a hurry at discharge. The report did not adjust for season or for changes in controller prescribing over the same period.

records.title: Written action plans for children with asthma: a systematic review of effects on urgent care use
records.authors: Rasmussen-Adu K, Petrov-Lindqvist E, Okafor-Grey J, Sato-Mbeki H
records.abstract: We searched four databases to 2019 for trials and controlled studies of written asthma action plans in children. Twelve studies with 3,105 children met the inclusion criteria. In seven randomised trials, action plans reduced urgent care visits (risk ratio 0.78, 95 percent CI 0.64 to 0.95), with substantial heterogeneity between trials. Plans based on symptoms and plans based on peak flow performed similarly. No study examined how complete the plans were, and only two measured whether families still had the plan at follow-up. Most trials delivered plans together with structured education, so the effect of the written plan alone is uncertain.

records.title: Measuring the completeness of paediatric asthma action plans: development and reliability of a five-item score
records.authors: Mwangi-Laurent A, Oduya-Fischer P, Castellanos-Webb D
records.abstract: We developed a five-item completeness score for paper asthma action plans covering daily medicines, signs of worsening, yellow-zone actions, emergency criteria and a booked follow-up appointment. Two respiratory educators independently scored 240 scanned plans. Agreement was good for the total score (kappa 0.81) and lowest for the yellow-zone item (kappa 0.64), where handwritten doses were often illegible. Only 38 percent of plans scored five of five. Scoring took about two minutes per plan. We recommend treating an illegible dose as missing and reporting item-level completeness alongside the total score.

records.title: Understanding of asthma action plans among caregivers with limited English proficiency
records.abstract: We assessed 152 caregivers of children discharged after an asthma admission, using a teach-back task on the yellow zone of the family's own plan. Caregivers who preferred a language other than English described the correct yellow-zone steps in 44 percent of cases, compared with 79 percent of English-preferring caregivers. Plans had been written in English for all families, and an interpreter had been used at discharge for 21 of 58 families who needed one. Caregivers with lower health literacy scores were also less accurate. The study was done at one children's hospital and did not follow children for later emergency visits.

records.title: Where do children go after an asthma discharge? Emergency revisits outside the discharging hospital
records.abstract: Using provincial emergency department data, we followed 3,880 children discharged after an asthma admission from two children's hospitals. Within 90 days, 17 percent had at least one asthma-related emergency visit. Of these revisits, 21 percent took place at a hospital other than the discharging one, most often a community hospital closer to home. Children from the lowest neighbourhood income quintile were more likely to revisit elsewhere. Studies that count only revisits to the discharging hospital would miss about one revisit in five and would under-count revisits most among lower-income families, biasing comparisons that differ by income.

records.title: Confounding by severity in observational studies of asthma discharge interventions
records.authors: Lindqvist-Oyelaran M, Adeyemi-Holt B, Tanaka-Reid F
records.abstract: We examined 14 observational studies of discharge interventions for childhood asthma, including action plans, education sessions and follow-up calls. In 11 studies, children who received the intervention differed from those who did not in markers of severity or family engagement, most often previous admissions and controller use. Only four studies adjusted for a measure of prior health care use, and none used an active comparator or a negative control outcome. We describe a minimum adjustment set (age, previous admissions in 12 months, admission severity, controller at discharge and area income) and recommend a negative control outcome such as injury visits.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. One provincial cohort found fewer 90-day emergency revisits after a complete plan (adjusted hazard ratio 0.72), and a review of seven trials supports written plans in general, though no trial measured completeness. A reliable five-item completeness score exists. One fifth of revisits happen at other hospitals, so linkage to provincial data is needed, and observational studies of discharge interventions are prone to confounding by severity and engagement. Caregivers who prefer another language understand English plans less well. The evidence supports a linked cohort with a pre-specified adjustment set, not a claim that completeness causes fewer revisits.
response.gradeRationale: One directly relevant observational cohort, a review of trials that did not measure completeness, and single-site measurement and equity studies; consistent direction but serious risk of confounding and indirectness.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; five source-derived claims with passages; overall certainty low.

response.reading: A complete plan sits between the admission and the 90 days at home, but so do severity, previous admissions, controller medicine and family circumstances, which also shape who gets a complete plan. Revisits are only fully visible through provincial linkage because one in five happens elsewhere, most often for lower-income families. Language preference affects whether a complete plan is usable. The measurement tool exists; the missing piece is a linked, adjusted comparison in this hospital's population.

response.procedures: Two respiratory educators score plans using the five-item score after a calibration set of 30 plans; 10 percent are double-scored. After the data sharing agreement is signed, the provincial custodian links the cohort by health number and returns revisits and readmissions within 90 days as a de-identified file.

response.designSummary: Cohort of first discharges per child; time to first asthma emergency revisit or readmission within 90 days; complete versus incomplete plan.
response.sampleSize: About 620 asthma admissions a year give about 2,480 discharges over four years and about 1,900 first discharges per child. With a 16 percent 90-day revisit risk, about 300 events are expected. If 45 percent of plans are complete, 300 events give 80 percent power at two-sided alpha 0.05 to detect a hazard ratio of about 0.72 (Schoenfeld approximation); a hazard ratio of 0.80 would need about 640 events, roughly eight years of discharges. The estimate will be reported with its confidence interval, not as a significance verdict.
response.primaryAnalysis: Cox model for time to first asthma emergency revisit or readmission within 90 days, adjusted for the seven pre-specified covariates, with robust standard errors; proportional hazards checked with scaled Schoenfeld residuals.
response.secondaryAnalysis: The same model for 90-day readmission and 30-day revisit; the negative control outcome; the association by caregiver language preference as a pre-specified interaction (h2); item-level completeness described without testing.
response.missingData: Plans missing from the scan archive are reported and treated as not assessed, never as incomplete; covariates missing for more than 5 percent of children are handled by multiple imputation with 20 imputations; children who move out of the province are censored at the last provincial contact.
response.multiplicity: One primary contrast; secondary outcomes and the language interaction are labelled as secondary and reported with confidence intervals only.
response.software: R with the survival package; code and covariate list archived before the linked file is received.
overfittingGuards: About 40 events per covariate for the primary model
response.summary: About 300 expected events give 80 percent power for a hazard ratio of about 0.72; smaller effects would need more years of discharges.

response.risks: Minimal physical risk; the main risk is privacy harm from linking identifiable charts to provincial emergency data.
response.consent: Individual consent is impracticable for about 1,900 past discharges; the REB approved a waiver of consent for secondary use (REB-2026-0871), with notice on the hospital's research transparency page.
response.data: Linkage by the provincial custodian using health numbers under the data sharing agreement; the analysis file holds no names, health numbers or exact dates and stays on the hospital research server.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: caregivers who prefer a language other than English, families in the lowest income quintile and children from rural areas who revisit community hospitals are the groups most likely to be missed or misclassified. The outcome is counted across hospitals, language preference and interpreter use are recorded, and results are reported by language group and income quintile.
response.effectiveness: The study informs whether an electronic plan with forced fields is worth funding; a precise null result is also useful.
response.efficiency: Uses existing charts and linked data, about 65 educator hours and 0.2 FTE of analyst time.
response.costs: Staff time within existing roles; a linkage fee from the custodian may apply and is not yet known.
response.grants: None needed for the cohort; a positive result would support a grant for a comparison of electronic and paper plans.
response.partnerships: Respiratory educators, two parent partners from the hospital's family advisory council, the provincial data custodian and a community hospital emergency physician.
response.rebPath: Approved by the hospital REB under TCPS 2 with a waiver of consent (REB-2026-0871); the data sharing agreement with the custodian is a separate requirement and no linkage starts before it is signed.
response.limitations: Residual confounding by family engagement; plans missing from the archive; revisits outside the province are not captured.
response.summary: Secondary use under an approved waiver, a separate unsigned data sharing agreement, and reporting by language and income.

response.partnershipPlan: Two parent partners review the completeness definition and the plain-language summary; a respiratory educator and a community hospital emergency physician review the outcome definitions before linkage.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; the family advisory council's notes on discharge teaching from the last year are read for themes about action plans.

response.title: Written asthma action plan completeness at discharge and emergency revisits within 90 days in children: a linked cohort study
response.abstract: Objective: to estimate the association between a complete written asthma action plan at discharge and asthma emergency revisits or readmissions within 90 days. Design: cohort of first asthma discharges per child from 2022 to 2025 at one children's hospital, linked to provincial emergency visit data. Exposure: five of five plan sections complete. Outcome: first asthma emergency visit or readmission at any provincial hospital. Results and conclusions will be written after linkage and analysis.
response.introduction: Written action plans reduce urgent care use in trials, but plans are often incomplete in practice, and revisits to other hospitals are invisible to the discharging team. Whether completeness itself matters is unknown for this population.
response.methods: Plans are scored with a five-item completeness score by educators blind to outcomes. Revisits and readmissions come from the provincial dataset after linkage. A Cox model adjusts for seven pre-specified covariates; injury visits serve as a negative control outcome.
response.results: No data have been analysed yet. The report will present the cohort flow, completeness by section, events at the discharging and other hospitals, crude and adjusted hazard ratios, the negative control result and the association by language group.
response.discussion: The discussion will weigh the estimate against the retrieved provincial cohort and the trials of written plans, and consider how much of any association could reflect family engagement rather than the plan itself. It will state what the result means for funding an electronic plan with forced fields.
response.limitations: Residual confounding by family engagement is likely, and plans missing from the archive may not be missing at random. Revisits outside the province are not captured, and the study covers one children's hospital.
response.conclusion: To be written after analysis. It will describe an association and will not claim that completeness causes fewer revisits.
response.summary: STROBE and RECORD structured draft; results left empty until the linked analysis.

path.problem.rawNeed:
I am a paediatric respirologist and the physician lead for the asthma pathway at a 190-bed children's hospital. We admit about 620 children aged 2 to 17 with asthma each year. Every child is supposed to go home with a written asthma action plan on our five-section paper template (daily medicines, signs of worsening, what to do in the yellow zone, when to come back to emergency, and a booked follow-up appointment), which is scanned into the chart. When our respiratory educator looked at 90 plans from last winter, 41 were missing at least one section, most often the yellow-zone steps or the follow-up appointment.

Our families come back a lot: roughly one in six children has another asthma visit to an emergency department within 90 days, and some of those visits are to the community hospitals nearer home, which we never hear about. Before we spend money on an electronic plan with forced fields, I want to know whether a complete plan at discharge is actually associated with fewer emergency revisits and readmissions within 90 days, or whether complete plans simply go to families who were going to do well anyway.

We would like to do a cohort study of discharges from 2022 to 2025, with plan completeness scored from the scanned template and revisits taken from the provincial emergency visits dataset so that visits to other hospitals are counted. I need help defining completeness, choosing the confounders that matter (severity of the admission, previous admissions, age, controller medicine at discharge, neighbourhood income), checking whether four years of discharges give enough events, and working out what we can say if the linkage is delayed. Our ethics approval is in place, but the data sharing agreement with the provincial custodian is not.
path.problem.constraints: No new funding. The analysis is done by me and a data analyst at 0.2 FTE over six months. Data come only from the hospital chart archive and the provincial emergency visits dataset; there is no contact with families.
